fragments.text: Hello, my name is Laura Kupe, and I'm a visiting fellow for geostrategic competition at New America and nonpartisan think tank based in Washington, D.C. My talk is called Unleashing Africa's AI potential from mineral to innovation. As the UN General Assembly convenes towards 80th session, world leaders face ongoing conflicts and need to re-evaluate multilateralism and accelerating institutional reforms all during a moment when artificial intelligence or AI is reshaping every dimension of human life. With AI reshaping every dimension of human life, its benefits, however, aren't reaching everyone equally. Today we explore critical question, will AI bridge the global divide or will it widen it for the long term? The numbers tell an interesting and sometimes a stark story, AI's economic rewards are

heavily concentrated in a handful of powerful tech companies and countries in the global north. Say a Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and a few others control the majority of AI development and deployment. These companies collectively command market for valuations and the trillions, while their AI models are trained on data extracted from all around the world, yet the economic benefits remain concentrated in Silicon Valley, Seattle, or other tech hubs. Meanwhile, much of the global south remains on the sidelines of this technological revolution. The risk, AI could become another force that intensifies global inequality or inequity, or imbalances, just like previous technological shifts. We've seen this pattern before, the industrial revolution, the internet boom, the mobile revolution. Each time promising universal benefits, yet consistently leaving out vulnerable communities

further behind, wherever they may be. Without deliberate intervention, AI risks intensifying global inequality, a warning underscored by UN Secretary General Antonio Voteres, who urged, seizing this, and I quote, historic opportunity to lay the foundation for inclusive governance of AI, for the benefit of all humanity. Nowhere is this challenge more apparent than in Africa, I'm a U.S. citizen with roots in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which is extremely rich in natural resources. Currently, the DRC is at the center of key global powers, vying for mineral riches, which include cobalt and copper, critical components at the heart of the fourth industrial revolution, or control of these minerals determines technological primacy in a age of AI, quantum computing,

and demands for just energy transition. This story, however, creates some irony as well, or this reality, in fact, the very minerals that power AI infrastructure are extracted from African soil, while the continent sees little benefit from the very AI revolution in technologies they enable. Congo, like the rest of the continent, stands as a crossroads, historically not having had the ability to benefit from the post-World War II economic order, but AI presents an unprecedented opportunity for the continent to make a leap forward, consider the scale of Africa's potential. That being, let's look at agriculture, agriculture employs approximately 60% of Africa's workforce. That's over 400 million people whose livelihoods could be transformed through technology.

Imagine revolutionizing the sector through AI-powered crop monitoring, disease detection, precision farming, and market forecasting. The African development bank reveals Africa's enormous potential. It includes 65% of the world's uncultivated arable land, abundant freshwater resources, and close to 300 annual sunny days. These are the perfect ingredients for AI-driven agricultural transformation that could not just feed Africa, but address global food security. The African Union's 2024 Continental AI Strategy recognizes this potential in agriculture as well. Highlighting AI deployment for crop disease identification, weather prediction, and enabling financial services and access to financial resources for farmers. But strategy alone isn't enough. Of course, we need implementation at scale. To truly understand AI's transformative potential, we need to look at the stories already

unfolding on the ground. In Kenya, AI-powered mobile applications help farmers detect crop diseases simply by taking a photo of their phones, reducing crop loss, and boosting food security for entire communities. Farmers who once lost entire harvests to preventable diseases now receive instant diagnosis and treatment recommendations. In Nigeria, AI's revolutioning financial inclusion by analyzing non-traditional data, including mobile phone uses, social connections, and even farming patterns, allowing small-scale entrepreneurs to secure financing that they typically would not reach. This creates a new class of micronsprenures who are driving local economic growth. In Ghana, AI-powered educational platforms are delivering personalized learnings to students in remote villages, and also just using basic smartphones to access world-class educational

content. Children who would otherwise have limited educational opportunities are now competing academically with their urban counterparts. And again, this is also a workforce that could be leveraged for Africa's agricultural sector. But there is a catch. The infrastructure needed to support this transformation currently does not exist. The statistics are sobering and reveal the magnitude of the challenge. 33% of Africa's internet connectivity, meaning 600 million people remain digitally disconnected. 43% of the population on the African continent lacks access to electricity, the most essential foundation for any AI deployment. These aren't just numbers, they represent real human potential locked away. How can farmers use AI-powered crop monitoring without reliable internet? How can communities benefit from smart agriculture without electricity to power the devices?

How can students access AI-enhanced education when schools lack basic connectivity? This infrastructure gap represents both the greatest challenge and opportunity for the African continent. Closing it could unlock Africa's AI potential and create a model for inclusive technological development worldwide. The cost of universal internet access across Africa is estimated at 100 billion by 2030, according to World Bank. And that is a fraction of what tech companies spend on AI development annually. Small-scale success stories are already merging on the continent about a path forward. They are solar-powered communities that are providing access to rural communities. I also mention again how farmers are using basic smartphones for weather forecasting and accessing real-time market pricing.

Mobile money platforms are also again enabling financial inclusion without traditional banking infrastructure. These are building blocks of transformation proof that with the right approach, technology can indeed serve everyone. So how do we ensure AI-led growth reaches everyone? How do we prevent AI from becoming another tool of exclusion? That is a very important question. And I have some recommendations or enabling frameworks to help reshape that thinking. So one thing I think about is first, how can international governance models facilitate technology transfer? This can be done, in my opinion, by building local capacity. This isn't about dependence, it's about empowerment. Countries need to develop their own AI expertise, train their own engineers, and create their

own AI solutions tailored to local needs. Not just consume AI products, developed elsewhere. This means investing in education. Second, there should be public-private partnerships that prioritize digital infrastructure for underserved communities, not just profitable urban centers. Two often, technology will allow its focus on urban markets while ignoring rural populations that need the most. We need business models that make serving everyone economically viable, not just serving the wealthy. Third, regional approaches to AI governance like the African-Unions Continental AI strategy need to become the norm. So by pooling resources and expertise and maintaining technological sovereignty over AI innovation regions can chart their own course. These approaches recognize, or these ideas are recommendations, recognize that one size

doesn't fit all, different regions have different needs, different strengths, different cultural context, and different visions. The path forward requires a fundamental shift in perspective. We must move beyond viewing the global south as a passive participant, but being an active partner in A.I.'s future across Africa, young innovators are already developing A.I. solutions focused on local needs. Not this grassroots innovation need support from forums like the United Nations. The global south must be a meaningful voice in shaping A.I. government frameworks, data sharing agreements and ethical standards, not just implementing decisions made in Washington, Brussels or Beijing. Success will be measured not by how quickly A.I. spreads but how accurately its benefits

are distributed, kind of farmer and rural Congo access the same A.I. tools as a corporate farm in California. Kind of student and LEGOs receive the same quality of A.I. in-hands education as one in London, because an entrepreneur and Nairobi compete in equal footing with startups in Silicon Valley. The choice is clear and urgent, A.I. can either be a force that divides our world or between the connected or the disconnected, or in the empowered and the disempowered. As the UN General Assembly continues its deliberations, the stakes couldn't be higher. The decisions made in these halls won't just shape the future of A.I. they'll determine whether the future includes everyone or leaves billions behind.

The historic opportunity sector General Guterres spoke of is real, but it's also fragile. Opportunities to build whosys systems don't last forever. Every day we delay action and the A.I. divide grows wider. The time is to act now, the choices we make today will determine whether A.I. becomes a tool for short progress or if it, you know, deep its division. And my hope is that as a collective we can see and work together how A.I. becomes a tool that shares progress and prosperity.
